title: Qwenputer: a fully functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
author: Divyansh Agrawal (independent)
more_note: Part 1 of 3 in the author's Qwenputer series; unchanged between the first archived copy (28 October) and 27 November. Its Try it section has the three commands that run the model.
takeaway: In one blog post with released code and weights, a compiler sets the weights of 11 extra layers (about 1M nonzero weights) in front of an unchanged Qwen3.5-4B so that Gated DeltaNet heads, with gate 1, write strength 1 and one-hot keys, act as exact RAM for a RISC-V (RV32IM) CPU. Qwen calls it through its tool-call format; on four 40-problem DeepMind arithmetic sets (greedy, one run each) it lands within one problem of base Qwen given the same tool answered on the host, and above base Qwen without tools (mul_big 97.5% against 55%). It runs through a custom driver, not plain generate(), and the post's NUPA 100% figure is from the earlier CHIP-8 version.
verdict: Believe the mechanism and its exactness: the RAM trick is plain linear algebra, and the released code checks the circuit against riscv-tests, qemu and a reference machine over millions of instructions. Read the benchmarks as parity with a host-side tool on small sets, with one bar from a different model, and read "no runtime" as "nothing outside the weights computes the answer": a custom driver boots the CPU, routes its trace tokens past Qwen and, in the measured runs, executes the compiled layers with a Triton re-implementation checked bit-equal to them.

headline.k: a 32-bit RISC-V CPU (RV32IM, Zba, a bignum unit) set by a compiler, no training, in front of Qwen3.5-4B's own 32 layers
headline.d: about 1.04M nonzero weights; passes riscv-tests and matches qemu
headline.at: it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32

headline.k: DeepMind mul_big, 40 problems, greedy: base Qwen3.5-4B (22/40) against Qwenputer (39/40)
headline.d: base Qwen with the same tool answered on the host: 40/40

headline.k: in about 230,000 output positions of the evaluation runs replayed against a reference model of the machine
headline.d: exactness of the circuit against its own reference, not of every answer
headline.at: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions

code.n: The compiler, the RISC-V core, the RvChat driver, the evaluation scripts and the design log (experimental/riscv/docs/rv32.md: every measurement, phase by phase). Code MIT; weights Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face (divagr1925/Qwen3.5-4B-Qwenputer, 18.8 GB) and ModelScope. Read at commit 0cab570 (9 November).

discussion.t: Hacker News: "Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5"

responses.t: "A custom host runtime is still responsible for loading firmware" (Hacker News comment)
responses.n: The host loads the firmware, boots the CPU and, while it runs, skips Qwen's own layers by hand; calls the "no external runtime" and "not a plugin" claims a little dishonest for that reason. The code confirms the description (RvChat), and the post itself lists the driver under its limits.

responses.t: "Ordinary causal attention can do exactly the same thing" (Hacker News comment)
responses.n: The RAM does not need a recurrent layer: attention can store and look up exact values too, at a memory cost that grows with the number of accesses instead of staying fixed. Correct, and the post's own claim is only that the recurrent version is cheaper.

responses.t: Qwenputer, an experimental model that treats Gated DeltaNet state as RAM to put a RISC-V CPU in its weights (in Korean)
responses.n: Reads the repository's history: the chart's NUPA bar is the CHIP-8 version's 576-problem result (the commit of 22 October says so, the next one removes the label); a McNemar column, with p = 1.0 for add_or_sub_big, was added and dropped on 19 October; the base column was re-run on 21 October; a firmware bug was fixed and the "never printed a wrong result" line dropped on 20 October. Each point checked here against the commits.

responses.t: A Developer Compiled a Full RISC-V CPU Into Qwen3.5's Weights
responses.n: A news write-up, not a rebuttal: its takeaways repeat "no external runtime" and the NUPA 100% figure, while its body says the prototype "requires a custom runtime" and a driver that loads firmware and hides the trace. Shows how the post's two framings travel side by side.

resources.t: Hybrid models can hide reasoning in their RNN state
resources.by: Divyansh Agrawal, 22 October 2026 (the author; Part 2 of the series)
resources.n: The first follow-up: fine-tuned to answer with no visible reasoning, OLMo-Hybrid (write strength allowed up to 2) learns to track a flipping switch silently and generalises to 256 flips; Qwen3.5 (write strength capped at 1 by a sigmoid) does not. Uses the same compiler for its probes.

resources.t: Building oversight tools into a model's weights
resources.by: Divyansh Agrawal, 22 October 2026 (the author; Part 3 of the series)
resources.n: The second follow-up: a linear lie probe whose trigger and log are compiled into the weights (91% of lies flagged, no false flags in 28,000 tokens of chat and GSM8K, the log kept in DeltaNet state), and a planted mechanism as an answer key for interpretability tools.

resources.t: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
resources.n: The paper the post cites for the delta rule as an associative memory; our owner page teaches the rule from it.

resources.t: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
resources.n: The layer Qwen3.5 uses three times in every four, with the gate and write strength this post pins to 1.

resources.by: Christos Tzamos and others, Percepta, 11 March 2026 (third-party; linked in the Hacker News thread)
resources.n: Earlier work on executing programs inside transformer weights (a WebAssembly interpreter), with its own fast decoding; Qwenputer's difference is that it sits beside an unchanged pretrained model that calls it.

resources.t: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability
resources.n: The best-known earlier compiler from a program to transformer weights (RASP programs); background for the compiler in section 3, which the post does not cite.
The base model: 32 layers, 24 of them Gated DeltaNet (16 key heads, 32 value heads, 128 x 128 states).

since.t: QwenFX: a coding agent inside the model
since.n: Vercel's fx coding agent, compiled unmodified, runs on the in-weights CPU with Qwen3.5-4B as its model: 15 of 15 small repository tasks, a new executor at about 24,000 trace tokens a second on an L4, the computer as a 125 MB chip file beside base Qwen. The host still renders the chat template, keeps the files and does the git work (the author's README, read 27 November).

since.t: Qwenputer-npu and QwenPU: neural networks on the in-weights CPU
since.n: Three added instructions (int8-by-int4 dot products) let Karpathy's 260K-parameter stories260K Llama run as a C program on the CPU, about 41 s a story token on an L4; QwenPU's vector unit cuts that to about 16 s, with a 26.7 GB checkpoint (the repository README, read 27 November).

kb.t: Beyond attention: SSMs, Mamba, linear attention, RWKV and hybrids
kb.n: Owns the delta rule, the gate and Gated DeltaNet (sections 3 and 6): the update this post pins to an exact RAM write.
Owns the Qwen line and its 3:1 hybrid of Gated DeltaNet and gated attention; Qwen3.5-4B is the base model here.
Residual stream, attention and MLP sublayers: the parts the compiler writes a CPU into.

kb.t: Building a harness: the loop, tool calling, edit formats, stop conditions
kb.n: How a tool call normally runs on the host: what Qwenputer replaces with layers that write the tool response themselves.
The other direction: an LLM reading and editing trained weights, where Qwenputer compiles new ones by hand.
The issue that linked the post among the week's reads.
